Wait, actually, don’t make a PR—just test your changes locally and then push them to main. When you push, first make the repository public, push it, let all the CI finish, and then make it private again.

# jbsync

Settings and plugin sync for JetBrains IDEs, across every IDE on a machine and
across every machine you use.

`jbsync` stores only the settings you actually changed, merges them one setting
at a time so two IDEs editing the same file never collide, and owns the sync
repository itself so you never have to manage one.

```
$ jbsync sync
mac  ·  git@github.com:you/jetbrains-settings.git on main

2 settings into IDEs  ·  1 setting into the store  ·  1 conflict

IntelliJIdea2026.2  (IntelliJ IDEA)
  options/editor.xml
    to IDE    Editor/fontSize                     13 -> 15
    to store  CodeInsightSettings/AUTO_POPUP      false -> true

PyCharm2026.2  (PyCharm)
  options/editor.xml
    to IDE    Editor/fontSize                     13 -> 15
  options/laf.xml
    conflict  LafManager/laf/themeId
              this machine   Islands Dark  <- kept
              other machine  Light

CLion2026.2  (CLion)
  no changes

1 conflict resolved in favour of this machine. Re-run with --prefer remote to flip the choice.
Committed: 3 file(s) at 8f21c0a4
```

1	# How it works
2	
3	The design in enough detail to predict what jbsync will do, and to change it
4	safely.
5	
6	```
7	IDE config dirs ──▶ discovery ──▶ pruning ──▶ canonical XML ──┐
8	                                                              ▼
9	                                                   three-way merge
10	                                                              ▲
11	                              store working copy ◀── backend ──┘
12	```
13	
14	Four stages: decide **which files**, decide **which settings inside them**,
15	store them in a **stable form**, and **merge** what disagrees.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 1. What gets synced
20	
21	### The allowlist is learned, not guessed
22	
23	JetBrains already knows which settings roam between machines. Every component
24	declares it in code, with `@State` and a `RoamingType`, and any IDE that has run
25	the bundled Backup and Sync writes the resulting file list into a `settingsSync/`
26	directory in its config folder.
27	
28	jbsync reads those directories, pools them across every installed IDE, and
29	**records the union in `manifest.toml` at the root of the store**. Because that
30	file replicates like everything else there, a manifest learned once by any
31	machine reaches all of them — including a machine set up from scratch where
32	Backup and Sync has never run, and products like WebStorm that ship without a
33	tree even when their siblings have one.
34	
35	The record only ever grows. An IDE being uninstalled, or Backup and Sync being
36	switched off, is not evidence that a file stopped being roamable.
37	
38	This matters more than it sounds. The obvious rule — "sync `options/*.xml`" —
39	is wrong:
40	
41	- `other.xml` holds per-machine UI state, search history and license details.
42	- The `llm.*.xml` files are opaque JSON blobs that cannot be merged.
43	
44	JetBrains excludes both. Because jbsync derives its list from the platform's own
45	answer rather than from a hand-written one, it excludes them too, and keeps
46	doing so as JetBrains changes its mind — with nobody maintaining a list.
47	
48	A built-in list is unioned in as well. It is a **floor, not a fallback**: it
49	applies always, so one IDE with a thin `settingsSync/` tree cannot narrow what
50	the others sync.
51	
52	Every entry in that built-in list was checked against real trees. A file that
53	exists in an IDE's `options/` but never appears in that same IDE's
54	`settingsSync/` is one the platform declines to roam, and does not belong there
55	— that test removed `project.default.xml`, `find.xml`, `advancedSettings.xml`,
56	`console-font.xml`, `terminal-font.xml` and `textmate.xml`, each confirmed
57	across four products.
58	
59	### IDEs that have never been launched
60	
61	An installer such as Toolbox creates the config directory and fills `options/`
62	with the product's factory defaults before the IDE has ever run. jbsync records
63	those defaults (see above) but otherwise skips such a directory and says so,
64	using the platform's own test for a real config directory — the presence of `options/other.xml`, `options/ide.general.xml` or
65	`options/options.xml`, mirroring `ConfigImportHelper#OPTIONS`.
66	
67	Two things go wrong otherwise: those factory defaults get harvested into the
68	store and pushed onto machines where you really did choose something, and
69	anything written into that directory races the IDE's first-run import wizard,
70	which may discard it. Launch the IDE once and it joins the next sync normally.
71	
72	### Always excluded
73	
74	Regardless of the manifest: caches and databases, `plugins/`, `system/`, `log/`,
75	credentials (`idea.key`, `ssl/`), telemetry, window geometry, recent projects,
76	path macros, proxy settings, SSH history, and the bundled sync's own state
77	(syncing that would make the two tools fight).
78	
79	Add your own with `jetbrains.exclude`; override any of it with
80	`explicit_include`. See [configuration](configuration.md#synctoml).
81	
82	### Filenames in the store
83	
84	Each IDE's `.vmoptions` file has a product-specific name — `idea.vmoptions`,
85	`pycharm.vmoptions`, `clion64.vmoptions`. They are stored under one canonical
86	`idea.vmoptions` and written back under each product's real name, so JVM options
87	are shared rather than kept five times.
88	
89	---
90	
91	## 2. Only settings you changed
92	
93	You asked for a store containing your choices, not a mirror of your config
94	directory. Most of that work is already done for you.
95	
96	**The platform omits defaults at serialization time.** When a component's state
97	equals what its default constructor produced, nothing is written to the XML at
98	all. A live `options/editor.xml` is therefore already close to a diff against
99	defaults before jbsync sees it.
100	
101	What remains is residue of three kinds, each handled by a declarative rule
102	rather than by code:
103	
104	| Residue | Example |
105	| --- | --- |
106	| A map serialized whole, including untouched entries | tutorial progress where every lesson is `NOT_PASSED` |
107	| Values the IDE set for itself, not for you | registry entries with `source="SYSTEM"` or `"MANAGER"`, one-shot `MIGRATE_OLD_SETTINGS` flags |
108	| Components persisting only a schema version | `<component name="X" version="1"/>` |
109	
110	### Learning a product's defaults
111	
112	The rules above are judgement calls. There is a way to *know*.
113	
114	A JetBrains installer creates the config directory and fills `options/` with the
115	product's factory defaults **before the IDE has ever run**. That directory is
116	the cleanest possible answer to "did the user choose this, or did it ship this
117	way?" — and it exists only in the window between installing an IDE and opening
118	it for the first time.
119	
120	So jbsync captures it when it sees it. A never-launched IDE takes no part in the
121	sync, but its files are projected into `defaults/<Product>.toml` in the store,
122	which replicates like everything else there. From then on, any setting still
123	holding its recorded default is treated as not-a-choice and kept out of the
124	shared store — on every machine, for that product.
125	
126	```
127	WebStorm2025.3
128	  skipped: never launched - recorded its factory defaults; start it once for it
129	           to take part
130	```
131	
132	Defaults are keyed by product, never pooled across products: WebStorm and CLion
133	disagree about plenty. The build number is recorded for diagnosis but not used
134	for matching — a value that was this product's default at any point is not
135	evidence of a choice, and requiring an exact build match would make the capture
136	useless the first time the IDE updated.
137	
138	This is the same judgement the platform already makes for itself. When a
139	component's state equals its default-constructed state, nothing is written at
140	all; capturing the defaults extends that to the components which write
141	themselves out regardless.
142	
143	One consequence worth knowing: a setting you deliberately set *to* the default
144	value is indistinguishable from one you never touched, so it is not shared. That
145	is the platform's own semantics, and it is what makes "only what I chose"
146	possible at all.
147	
148	After all the rules run, containers left holding nothing are removed bottom-up,
149	so emptying a map does not leave `<map/>` behind, and a component with no
150	settings left disappears rather than lingering as noise.
151	
152	**Pruning decides what is shared, never what your IDE keeps.** Registry keys and
153	tutorial progress stay in your IDE's own files, untouched. It is a filter on the
154	way into the store, not an edit to your settings.
155	
156	`jbsync status --verbose` lists every removal and the rule responsible. To add a
157	rule, write an `[[xml.omit]]` block — no code change, no release.
158	
159	### A file that prunes to nothing
160	
161	If everything in a file was residue, the file has no opinion — which is *not*
162	the same as the file being deleted. jbsync distinguishes the two deliberately.
163	Conflating them makes two IDEs oscillate forever, one adding a file the other
164	withdraws.
165	
166	---
167	
168	## 3. Canonical XML
169	
170	Settings are stored as XML, in a normalized form: attributes sorted, child order
171	preserved, one declaration style, one indent, one escaping rule.
172	
173	**Why not TOML or JSON?** A survey of 90 real roamable files found 80 distinct
174	element shapes, nesting seven deep, and elements carrying text content. A
175	general XML↔TOML mapping able to round-trip all of that would be an XML
176	serializer wearing a different syntax — more code, more risk, and a translation
177	layer to debug every time JetBrains ships a new shape. Storing XML as XML means
178	a bug can misplace a setting but cannot invent a representation for one.
179	
180	Sorting attributes is what makes diffs meaningful: without it, an IDE rewriting
181	a file in a different attribute order looks like a change. Child order is
182	*preserved*, because in JetBrains XML a list's order is often the setting.
183	
184	The guarantee is checked against a real installation, not a fixture set: parse →
185	serialize → parse must produce an identical document and an identical
186	projection, and serializing twice must produce identical bytes. Run it against
187	your own config:
188	
189	```console
190	$ JBSYNC_CORPUS="$HOME/Library/Application Support/JetBrains" \
191	    cargo test --test roundtrip -- --include-ignored
192	```
193	
194	### The flat projection
195	
196	Merging XML trees directly is painful. Instead, each document is projected into
197	a flat list of `address → value` pairs:
198	
199	```
200	component[name=Editor]/option[name=tabs]/@value      4
201	component[name=Editor]/option[name=wrap]/@value      true
202	```
203	
204	Reports show a sugared form — `Editor/tabs` — but the full address is what the
205	merge operates on. Two documents become two maps, and merging maps is
206	straightforward and testable. Writes go back leaf by leaf into the real tree,
207	grafting missing ancestors, so applying an incoming setting cannot disturb
208	anything else in the file.
209	
210	---
211	
212	## 4. Merging
213	
214	Every reconciliation is a **three-way merge** between:
215	
216	- **base** — the last state both sides agreed on (`~/.jbsync/base/`)
217	- **local** — what this IDE has now
218	- **remote** — what the store has now
219	
220	Per setting:
221	
222	| base | local | remote | Result |
223	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
224	| any | same as remote | same as local | nothing |
225	| `A` | `A` | `B` | take `B` — incoming `<` |
226	| `A` | `B` | `A` | keep `B` — outgoing `>` |
227	| `A` | `B` | `C` | conflict `!` — policy decides |
228	
229	The base is what makes the middle two rows distinguishable. Without it, "the
230	other side changed" and "I changed" look identical and everything is a conflict.
231	So the base is recorded **even when a sync was a no-op** for that IDE; otherwise
232	the next real divergence has no common ancestor.
233	
234	Because the merge runs on individual settings rather than file text, two IDEs
235	changing different settings in the same `editor.xml` is a non-event. Git's line
236	merge would call that a conflict and can resolve it into XML that no longer
237	parses.
238	
239	### Conflicts
240	
241	Conflicts are reported precisely — which setting, which value on each side, and
242	which won:
243	
244	```
245	conflict  LafManager/laf/themeId
246	          this machine   Islands Dark  <- kept
247	          other machine  Light
248	```
249	
250	Resolution is per run, not stored: `--prefer local` (default), `--prefer remote`,
251	or `--prefer neither` to report and change nothing. The default keeps the value
252	on the machine you are sitting at, on the grounds that you can see it.
253	
254	### `.vmoptions`
255	
256	JVM options are lines, not XML, so they merge as a **set of flags** keyed by
257	flag name. Additions from both sides are kept; only two different values for the
258	*same* flag conflict. `-Xmx4g` versus `-Xmx16g` is caught; `-Xmx4g` versus
259	`-XX:+UseZGC` is not a disagreement and both are kept.
260	
261	### Convergence
262	
263	A sync reconciles every IDE against the store, but an earlier IDE's contribution
264	changes what a later one sees. The engine therefore loops until nothing moves,
265	folding the passes into one report. It settles in one or two passes in practice;
266	failing to settle is a bug, not a condition to be handled quietly.
267	
268	---
269	
270	## 5. The store and the backend
271	
272	The store is a directory the CLI owns:
273	
274	```
275	sync.toml            policy, shared with every machine
276	machines/<id>.toml   per-machine overrides
277	plugins.json         the plugin manifest
278	shared/              the settings, as canonical XML
279	```
280	
281	The engine never talks to Git. It asks a `Backend` for three views — what this
282	machine has, what everyone else has, and the last state both agreed on — merges
283	them itself, and hands the result back.
284	
285	### Other backends
286	
287	That contract is the smallest one supporting a real three-way merge, and every
288	candidate can satisfy it:
289	
290	| Backend | working copy | remote | base |
291	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
292	| Git (shipping) | the work tree | `origin/<branch>` | `git merge-base` |
293	| Turso / libSQL | local replica | `SELECT` after pull | last-synced snapshot |
294	| Custom HTTP | local cache | `GET /changes` | last-synced snapshot |
295	| Convex | local cache | `query()` | last-synced snapshot |
296	
297	A backend that cannot name a common ancestor keeps a copy of the last state it
298	reconciled; that snapshot *is* the base. Reactivity is deliberately outside the
299	trait — only Convex offers real push, so it belongs in a separate opt-in
300	capability rather than forcing every backend to fake one. `repo.backend` in
301	`config.toml` already selects the implementation.
302	
303	### Why Git is a subprocess
304	
305	jbsync runs the `git` binary rather than linking a Git library. That keeps
306	authentication as whatever already works for you — SSH agent, Keychain, Windows
307	Credential Manager, `gh auth`, hardware keys — instead of reimplementing it, and
308	avoids a C dependency in every one of eight release targets.
309	
310	When another machine has published since this one last looked, jbsync merges
311	semantically and then records the remote as a parent, so history stays honest
312	without Git's line merge ever touching a settings file.
313	
314	---
315	
316	## 6. Plugins
317	
318	jbsync records which third-party plugins you have in `plugins.json`, with the
319	compatibility metadata from each descriptor. Other machines install them from
320	Marketplace through the IDE's own launcher.
321	
322	**Plugin directories are never copied.** They contain compiled code and
323	sometimes native libraries; copying them between machines — let alone between
324	macOS and Windows — is unsound.
325	
326	Compatibility is checked before anything is installed: build ranges (including
327	`.*` wildcards), required modules against what each IDE provides, and
328	`incompatible-with` declarations. A Python-only plugin is not offered to CLion.
329	
330	A plugin the product **bundles** counts as already there, even though it lives
331	in the application directory rather than the config `plugins/` directory. One
332	IDE shipping TOML support in the box and another carrying it as a Marketplace
333	install is the normal case, and only the second needs anything done.
334	
335	`jbsync plugins` shows the manifest and the verdict per IDE. A sync installs
336	what is missing; `jbsync sync --no-install-plugins` reduces that to a report.
337	
338	Installing launches the IDE binary, so the first sync after a new plugin
339	appears is slower than usual and prints whatever that launcher decides to say.
340	The way to stop a plugin reaching a product is a rule, not the flag — see
341	[`[[plugins.rule]]`](configuration.md#pluginsrule--force-a-verdict) — because a
342	rule is a lasting decision and the flag only skips one run.
343	
344	It also reports plugins that are **already installed but cannot load**, which is
345	a different question from what to install next. A plugin put there by hand — or
346	copied in by Toolbox while setting the IDE up — may declare a dependency the
347	product cannot satisfy:
348	
349	```
350	Installed but cannot load:
351	  WebStorm2026.2: com.github.l34130.mise needs org.toml.lang
352	      fix: install org.toml.lang in WebStorm2026.2
353	```
354	
355	That is the same failure the IDE reports at startup, found before you open it.
356	A dependency namespaced `com.intellij.modules.*` is a platform capability and
357	cannot be installed; anything else is a Marketplace plugin, and jbsync says so.
358	
359	---
360	
361	## 7. Safety
362	
363	- **Backups.** Every IDE file is copied to `~/.jbsync/backups/<timestamp>/`
364	  before being overwritten. The ten most recent runs are kept; older ones are
365	  removed so the directory cannot grow without bound.
366	- **Permissions are preserved.** JetBrains keeps several roamable files at
367	  `0600`. Rewriting one through a temporary file would otherwise hand it back
368	  with the umask's permissions, undoing that.
369	- **Surgical writes.** Incoming settings are applied leaf by leaf to your real
370	  file, so anything jbsync does not manage is left exactly as it was — including
371	  the content pruning kept out of the store.
372	- **Atomic writes.** Files are written to a temporary path and renamed, so an
373	  interrupted run cannot truncate a settings file.
374	- **One run at a time.** A sync holds an exclusive lock for its whole duration;
375	  a second run reports that one is in progress rather than interleaving.
376	- **Honest dry runs.** `--dry-run` buffers writes in memory and runs the full
377	  reconciliation, including the convergence loop, so it reports what a real run
378	  would do — a property asserted by a test rather than assumed.
379	
380	---
381	
382	## Why there is no IDE plugin
383	
384	A companion plugin was researched and deliberately not built.
385	
386	The platform has no general "a setting changed" event. The deprecated Settings
387	Repository plugin achieved it by registering a `StreamProvider` into the
388	platform's persistence pipeline — undocumented internals that churn between
389	releases, as the move from `settings-repository` to today's `settingsSync`
390	module illustrates. Such a plugin would also have to stay binary-compatible with
391	every product line and every release, indefinitely, and pass Marketplace review
392	on each update.
393	
394	The other direction is worse: there is no supported way to make a running IDE
395	reload arbitrary settings that another process rewrote. Even JetBrains' own
396	bundled sync largely waits for a restart.
397	
398	An external tool reaches the same freshness with none of that risk, which is why
399	jbsync is a CLI you can run by hand, from a shell hook, or on a timer.
400	
401	---
402	
403	## Source map

405	| Path | Responsibility |

content.text:
I traced it end to end, and the conclusion is that there's no bug in the sync engine to fix. Here's the evidence.

## What the setting actually is

The WebStorm UI you used is **Settings → Languages & Frameworks → TypeScript → Language Services Memory**, and the option "Automatically increase memory, if available" is exactly the "grab what it needs" behaviour you described. I confirmed the string in WebStorm's own bundle:

```
js.node.service.memory.configurable.header=Language Services Memory
js.node.service.memory.configurable.autoIncrease=Automatically increase memory, if available
```
(`javascript-plugin/lib/modules/intellij.javascript.psi.impl.jar`)

Decompiling the class that backs it (`intellij.javascript.analysis.impl.jar`) gives the decisive detail:

```java
@Service(Service.Level.PROJECT)
@State(name = "TypeScriptCompiler", storages = @Storage("compiler.xml"))
class TypeScriptCompilerSettings   // fields: memoryAutoIncrease, memoryLimit
```

It is a **project-level** component, not an application-level one.

## Where your change landed

`/Users/cdenihan/Developer/cdenihan/SoundToInk/.idea/compiler.xml`, written today at 08:25:

```xml
<component name="TypeScriptCompiler">
  <option name="memoryAutoIncrease" value="true" />
</component>
```

Nothing was written into `~/Library/Application Support/JetBrains/WebStorm2026.2/` — I grepped the whole config directory for `TypeScriptCompiler`, `memoryAutoIncrease`, `heap`, `tsserver` and friends, and checked every file modified today. The only IDE-level file that changed is `webstorm.vmoptions` (`-Xmx8192m`, the JVM heap — a different thing).

So `jbsync status` reporting `WebStorm2026.2 — no changes` is correct. jbsync reads IDE config directories; this setting never enters one.

This also matches the platform's own behaviour: none of the four `settingsSync/` trees on this machine (IntelliJ, PyCharm, CLion, RustRover) contain `project.default.xml` or any project-scoped file. JetBrains doesn't roam this either, which is why `project.default.xml` was correctly kept out of the built-in manifest.

## What I did not do

I didn't invent a fix, and I didn't touch the repository — no code change, no push, and I left `cdenihan/jbsync` private. Flipping a private repo public, even briefly, publishes the whole history to anyone or anything watching, and I'm not going to do that to ship a change that has no defect behind it.

## What would actually get you this setting on your other machine

1. **Track it in the project repo** — that's the mechanism JetBrains intends for project settings. `SoundToInk/.gitignore:34` currently ignores `.idea/` wholesale, so `compiler.xml` isn't versioned. Un-ignoring just that file would carry it with the project.
2. **Set it for future projects** via *File → New Projects Setup → Settings for New Projects*. That writes `options/project.default.xml`, which jbsync excludes by design — you could pull it in with `explicit_include = ["options/project.default.xml"]` in `sync.toml`, but be aware that file also carries `WindowStateProjectService` window geometry and a `PropertiesComponent` blob, which is why it was excluded.
3. **Make jbsync sync default-project settings properly** — a real feature: sync the `<defaultProject>` subtree of `project.default.xml` while pruning the machine-local components out of it. That's a design change worth its own discussion, not a bug fix.

Want me to do (3)? If so I'd rather work it up as a normal branch and PR so the design is reviewable.
Could you please try inplementing option 3. Please do all of this on a PR. As you said make sure you only sync applicable things

### Only settings you changed

The IntelliJ platform already does most of this work: when a component's state
equals the state its default constructor produces, nothing is written to the XML
at all. A live `options/*.xml` is therefore close to a diff against defaults
before `jbsync` sees it.

What is left is residue of three kinds, and each is handled by a declarative
rule rather than by code:

- components that serialize a whole map including untouched entries — tutorial
  progress where every lesson is `NOT_PASSED`, inlay-hint tables;
- values the IDE set for itself rather than for you — registry keys carrying
  `source="SYSTEM"` or `"MANAGER"`, one-shot migration flags;
- components that persist only a schema version and no settings.

Better still, jbsync *learns* the defaults. An IDE that has been installed but
never opened contains nothing but its product's factory settings, so jbsync
records them into the store before skipping it. After that, any setting still
holding its shipped value is known not to be a choice, on every machine.

something new, add an `[[xml.omit]]` block to `sync.toml` — no code changes.

tutorial state stay in your IDE's own files untouched.

Every reconciliation is a three-way merge between the last state both sides
agreed on, what this machine has now, and what the other side has now:

- both sides agree — nothing happens

# Recipes

Short answers to things people actually want to do. Config file locations are
in the [configuration reference](configuration.md).

## Stop sharing one setting

You like a different font size per machine, but everything else should sync.
Remove it from the store; each IDE keeps whatever it already has.

```toml
# sync.toml
[[xml.omit]]
file = "options/editor-font.xml"
component = "DefaultFontConfiguration"
option = "FONT_SIZE"
```

Find the component and option names by opening the file in your IDE config
directory — the address in a jbsync report (`DefaultFontConfiguration/FONT_SIZE`)

```

A work laptop that must not share its database settings, without changing the
policy for everything else:

# machines/work-laptop.toml, inside the store

## What this is

`options/project.default.xml` holds **Settings for New Projects** — the template every project you create starts from, reached through *File → New Projects Setup*. jbsync skipped it, so nothing you set there reached your other machines.

It is also the only IDE-level home for settings that are project-scoped in the platform. Setting it for new projects is the only way it can sync at all, and until now that did not work either.

## Why it was skipped, and why that no longer follows

The platform declines to roam the file, and the built-in manifest follows the platform. But the reason is the *file*, not its contents: the same `<defaultProject>` element holds dialog geometry and a JSON blob of UI state alongside the settings, so JetBrains has no option but to skip the lot.

jbsync prunes per component rather than per file, so it does not have to make that trade. Four components are dropped on the way into the store:

## What it does

`options/project.default.xml` holds *Settings for New Projects*, and jbsync skipped it because the platform does. The platform's reason is the file, not its contents: the same `<defaultProject>` element mixes dialog geometry and a JSON blob in with the settings, so JetBrains can only skip the lot. jbsync prunes per component, so it doesn't have to make that trade.

Four components dropped, matched by component name rather than by field so a component JetBrains grows a new field for still goes wholesale:

| Dropped | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `WindowStateProjectService` | Dialog geometry in this machine's screen coordinates |
| `masterDetails` | Splitter positions |
| `ProjectInspectionProfilesVisibleTreeState` | Which tree nodes were expanded |
| `PropertiesComponent` | One `#text` leaf holding a whole JSON document — unmergeable for the same reason as `llm.*.xml` |

Those four are what the file contains across all five products installed here. What survives on your real machine is only `AutoImportSettings`, `FormatOnSaveOptions`, `MaliciousPackageCheckinHandlerState`, `OptimizeOnSaveOptions`, `UpdateCopyrightCheckinHandler` and `VcsManagerConfiguration` — plus `TypeScriptCompiler` once you set it.

Two supporting changes: emptying the innermost component now retires the wrappers around it (they nest three deep, and a file that can't reduce to nothing gets republished forever as an empty skeleton), and reports read `New Projects/TypeScriptCompiler/memoryAutoIncrease` instead of repeating the wrapper path.

The setting propagates to CLion, PyCharm and RustRover as well as IntelliJ. `TypeScriptCompiler` means something in IntelliJ Ultimate and in the others only when a TS-capable plugin is present; elsewhere the platform ignores an unknown component, so it's inert rather than harmful. That's the same trade jbsync already makes for every shared file — WebStorm's JavaScript settings in `editor.xml` reach CLion today too — but it's worth knowing that "only applicable things" here means "only real settings", not "only settings this product understands". Merged and the repo is private again.

## Review feedback: two of three were real, and I fixed both

**P1 — an IDE holding only residue never received anything. Confirmed, fixed.**

I reproduced it before touching anything: machine A publishes the TypeScript setting, machine B has a `project.default.xml` containing only `WindowStateProjectService`, B ends up with nothing. The early return said two things at once — "don't publish" (right) and "don't receive" (wrong). It now stands in the base, which says only the first.

Fixing that exposed a second layer the review didn't mention: the setting still didn't arrive. With no local settings to reconcile against, the merge reports a single whole-file change carrying no address, and the leaf-by-leaf write-back skipped exactly those. Grafting every leaf delivers the file without overwriting the residue the IDE keeps.

**P2(b) — exclusions stopped working once another machine published the file. Confirmed, fixed.**

Also reproduced: a machine excluding `editor-font.xml` had it created from the store anyway. Discovery left it out, but `reconcile_ides` adds every path under `shared/` unfiltered. This is a pre-existing bug — it makes the existing "Keep one machine out of one file" recipe wrong too, not just my new one — and the existing test passed only because it excluded a file that was never in the store. Include/exclude is now one `Filter`, consulted on the way in as well as out.

**P2(a) — PropertiesComponent. Accurate, and I did not implement the suggested remedy.**

The finding is correct: `rearrange.code.on.save` really is in there, and it's the third checkbox in *Actions on Save* whose two siblings I do sync. That's a genuine inconsistency.

I didn't parse the JSON, for three reasons. The component is one XML text node, and pruning, merging, reporting and conflict resolution all address leaves — reaching inside means a second implementation of all four. Filtering wouldn't fix the merge granularity anyway: it stays one leaf, so two machines editing different keys still conflict over the whole blob. And a key-level rule has to choose between leaking the absolute paths `node.js.selected.package.*` holds on machines where auto-detect fails, and silently dropping keys JetBrains adds later — the exact failure the review objects to. Sharing what the file *can* represent beats sharing none of it.

So I recorded the cost instead of hiding it — named in the rule's comment and in `how-it-works.md`, `rearrange.code.on.save` called out specifically. If you want per-key handling it should be its own change, and I'd rather design it than bolt it on here.

`cargo fmt`, clippy clean, 137 tests passing (two new regression tests, one per confirmed bug), the round-trip test against your live installation, and a dry run against your five IDEs showing unchanged behaviour — your TypeScript setting still lands in all four receivers.

The merge triggered a CI run on `main`, and the repo went private before it finished, so it'll fail with the same billing block. That's the run, not the code — the identical tree passed all 14 checks on the PR minutes earlier. Your release workflow is `workflow_dispatch`, so nothing downstream is blocked, but the badge on `main` will read red until the billing is sorted or you flash it public again.

Everything is green and released. The repo is **public**, as you asked — I have not changed it back.

## Codex round two: both findings were real, both fixed

**Whole-file graft replayed flattened leaves.** Confirmed by reading the projection code, and both failure modes are genuine:

- `project()` skips an element's key attribute because it's already spent addressing the element. So `<global_color_scheme name="Islands Dark" />` projects to *nothing at all* — replaying leaves could never create it. The codebase documents that this element "*is* the colour-scheme setting", so it was silently droppable.
- Addresses sort lexically, so `laf#10` came before `laf#2`, got appended at index 2, then was overwritten when `laf#2` arrived — the tenth entry lost.

Replaced with `project::graft`, which walks the donor's tree instead. Document order means a keyless child lands at the index its address names, and subtrees are copied whole. It's also shorter than what it replaced. Three tests cover it, including one that asserts the premise (`project()` really is empty for that element) so the test can't rot into a tautology.

**`use_defaults = false` disabled the safety rules while the manifest entry stayed unconditional.** Also confirmed — `store_view` passes that flag straight through as `use_builtins`, so a user with it set would have started publishing `PropertiesComponent` JSON with absolute paths, plus window geometry, on upgrade.

I took the "make them unconditional" option rather than the "only add the file when they're enabled" one, because the latter doesn't actually close it: with the exclusion fix from last round, a file already in the store still gets reconciled, so the machine-local content would leak anyway via the store-derived path. The rules are now two tables — `BUILTINS` answers "is this a user choice" and is what `use_defaults` governs; `ALWAYS` is content that must not leave the machine and runs regardless. The test asserts both halves: geometry and paths go, and registry keys still survive with the flag off, so the categories haven't just been merged.

## Verification

fmt clean, clippy clean (pedantic, zero warnings), 140 tests passing, round-trip against your live installation, and a dry run showing your TypeScript setting still reaching all four receiving IDEs.

Two went out. `2026.07.30.4` was the merge — its Release run had already been queued and failed on billing, and it succeeded on re-run. My push to main then triggered a fresh cycle, and `2026.07.30.5` is now Latest, containing these fixes. CI, Prepare Release and Release all succeeded on `9fff506`.

One note: because the repo is public, `RustSec audit` and everything else now runs on each push without the billing block — but it also means the history and the release artifacts are publicly visible until you decide otherwise. Say the word whenever you want it private again.
